lessons.t: Money Models 1 — Context (12 min)
lessons.md:
- Trilogy logic: Offers = what to sell; Leads = who to sell to / how to get them; **Money Models = how to get them to pay (more, faster) so you can advertise profitably.** Alex wrote this one first, then realized readers needed Offers and Leads before it. Education as legacy; his books are "apprenticeship at scale".
- **Problem it solves**: most advertising isn't profitable in time — e.g. LTGP $1,000 vs CAC $100 (10:1) is a great trade, but if the $1,000 arrives a year later you're cash-negative for 12 months and must burn savings, debt or equity. **Door #3: make more than CAC in gross profit within the first 30 days.**
- **Client-Financed Acquisition (CFA)**: gross profit from one customer in their first 30 days > the cost to acquire them → customers fund the acquisition of more customers; growth is no longer limited by your capital.
- Origin story: his first gym (a $5k/month lease, slept on the floor) grew to 9+ staff until Facebook raised his cost per lead ~5×. On a layover he met a college acquaintance whose supplement stores did ~$80k and ~$130k/month; Alex started reselling supplements — ~$200 per new member (~$100 profit) — which covered the cost of acquiring each member, so the memberships became pure profit. **"I was getting paid to get new customers."** Over time he went from ~4–5:1 to 30–40:1 returns; licensed the model to 5,000+ gyms via Gym Launch — average ~4:1 upfront in 30 days, before memberships. Goal of the course: never use your own money to get customers again.

lessons.t: Money Models 2 — How Businesses Make Money (5 min)
lessons.md:
- **LTGP must exceed CAC** — measured in gross profit, not revenue. Alex's meal business: $100 CAC, "$500 lifetime revenue" looked like 5:1, but at 20% margins = ~$33 GP in month 1 and ~$100 lifetime — a loss after overhead. 80% of complaints came from meals vs 95% of profit from supplements → he shut meals down.
- **Benchmark: LTGP:CAC ≥ 3:1 as the bare minimum** (that meal business needed ~$1,500 LTGP).
- **The only three numbers that matter**: **CAC** (cheap customers), **gross profit** (lots of money per customer), **payback period** (fast). Goal: more money, faster.

lessons.t: Money Models 3 — CAC (23 min)
lessons.md:
- **CAC = all costs to sell new customers ÷ number of new customers**: ad spend, media buyer/creative payroll, software, sales commissions/salaries, managers. (Optionally track "media CAC" vs "fully loaded CAC".) Examples: outreach — $3k emailer + $200software+8×$100 commissions = $4k ÷ 8 = **$500**; content — 2×$5kmediateam+10×$100 = $11k ÷ 10 = **$1,100**; paid ads — $4k buyer + $20k media + $1ksoftware+10×$1k commissions = $35k ÷ 10 = **$3,500**. Measuring a metric is the first way to improve it.
- Biggest CAC levers: **better offers** (more responses, higher conversion, cheaper CPMs); cheaper labour/software are minor and hurt morale.
- **Free and new are the two most powerful words in advertising.** Dan Ariely's Hershey's Kiss test: free vs 1 cent → ~9× more takers (the "penny gap"). Give away value free (content, tools, lead magnets) — Chick-fil-A rule: free or full price, never in between.
- If people don't take your free thing: it's the wrong thing / described wrong, they **don't believe it** (a marketer's yearly "send $100, get $1,000" ad got no calls; "make an extra $500/month" can out-convert "$5,000/month" because it's believable), or the wrong people see it.
- Free brings volume — if you can't handle it, **add friction** (qualifying questions, more steps, tighter targeting, required pre-consumption, longer ads) rather than weakening the offer.
- **"Free brings broke people" is a myth**: Gym Launch tested ~10 free-ad vs ~10 non-free locations repeatedly — **close rates were identical**; free locations just paid far less per lead. Good reps close both, bad reps close neither.
- "If I had one offer to make or my family dies, it'd be free." **Create flow → monetize → add friction** — you can't optimize an empty inbox.
- **Discounts** sit on the same continuum as free. Skip moderate discounts (10–20% doesn't change behaviour — only loses margin); go **≥50% on something people already know the value of**. For high-cost-per-no-show businesses (dentist, lawyer, chiro) use a small paid discount to get a **card on file** (no-show fees; seamless upsell "use the card on file?") or have a junior person take free first appointments.
- **4 ways to display the same discount** (rotate to keep ads fresh): % off, $ off, relative equivalent ("less than a lunch out"), portion off ("4 months free"), or crossed-out retail next to the price. Dollar prices like "$29adjustment"or"$20 teeth whitening" work only where the market knows the normal price; for intangible/unique products, use % off a retail anchor.
- Never discount the whole core service with hard costs — **splinter off one well-understood piece** and discount that. Bargain hunters are still easier to upsell than cold prospects.

lessons.t: Money Models 4 — Gross Profit (10 min)
lessons.md:
- **GP = price − cost of goods sold** (variable costs per unit/customer only — not rent, admin, utilities; staff delivery cost is allocated per client). Gross margin = GP as a percentage.
- CAC between competitors is usually similar (e.g. $2.5k vs $3.5k); the gap between "whales and minnows" is **value per customer**. The consulting-day story: same unit sales as Alex, ~1/56th of the profit ($300kvs~$17M/year). **"Gross profit is the arms race of business"** — Dan Kennedy: whoever can spend the most to acquire a customer wins; Alex's version: whoever makes the customer most valuable to their business wins → "ethical monopoly" via outbidding. Cost can only go down to zero; value per customer can go up without limit (the $50k burger story).
- Examples: product $100 − $20 = $80 GP. Service: $3k/month clients, one $6k/month rep per 10 clients → $600 cost per client → $2,400 GP = 80% margin. **Service businesses need ≥80% gross margin to scale** (≈ cost × 5 price) — after rent, admin, ads, you may net ~30%.
- Easiest GP levers without changing price/cost: **more** (quantity/duration — bulk, buy again), **better** (higher quality version), **new** (complementary add-on — fries and a Coke, then supersize).

lessons.t: Money Models 5 — Payback Period (10 min)
lessons.md:
- **Payback period = how long until cumulative gross profit exceeds CAC** (break-even time; a.k.a. cash conversion cycle). The shorter it is, the faster you can recycle the same dollars into more ads — and the less you need a "marketing budget".
- Don't feel guilty making several offers: buyers move in short **hyper-buying windows** (a new decision/identity — e.g. someone who buys a bike to lose weight then buys helmet, shoes, clothes, bottles and signs up for a race within a day or two). If you don't offer, a competitor collects. Making offers ≠ hard selling; you sell 0% to people who don't know you sell it.
- Worked example: CAC $160, price $100/month, COGS $20 → GP $80/month → break-even in **month 2**. Always calculate with GP, not revenue.
- Improve it with more/better/new offers **inside the first 30 days, at the right moment**. **Sell at the point of greatest deprivation, not greatest satisfaction** (a second steak after a steak dinner doesn't sell). Alex's supplements flopped when pitched right after the membership sale (itch already scratched); they sold once he booked a nutrition orientation 48 hours later, reviewed the client's food and created a new problem that supplements solved.
- **5 upsell moments**: (1) **immediately** in the same conversation (works when solving problem A naturally opens problem B); (2) **next step**, 24–72 hours later (an orientation/consult that surfaces the new problem); (3) **after the first big win** (a solved problem opens a fully formed new one — e.g. hitting $10k/month creates tax and hiring problems); (4) **halfway point** (empirically very receptive); (5) **last chance / exit** — most businesses only try here, which is the worst time. Move offers earlier — "keep the party going".
- Quick fixes: charge **first + last month today**, or add an initiation / onboarding / enrollment / activation fee (pure GP). In the example this pulls payback from 2 months to ~1.5 and within 30 days.

lessons.t: Money Models 6 — Client-Financed Acquisition: the 3 levels of advertising (7 min)
lessons.md:
- **Level 1: LTGP > CAC** (ideally ≥3×) — minimum to be a real business.
- **Level 2: 30-day GP > CAC** → you never spend your own money to grow. Why 30 days: almost any business can get ~30 days of interest-free money (credit card / credit line). Buy customers on the card, pay it off from their first-month GP, repeat. You'll hit **operational limits before advertising limits**. Limit: still capped by your credit limit.
- **Level 3: 30-day GP > 2× CAC** → never limited by money. Each customer repays their own acquisition and funds the next one, so acquisition compounds per customer (1→2→4→8…); reinvesting monthly at 2× gives ~4,000 customers by month 12. More than 2× (3×, 5×, 10×) compounds faster. Alex's first year of Gym Launch: ~**100:1** return (~$100kadspend→~$10M); limits were market size and delivery capacity. Most people move on from fixing the money model too soon.

lessons.t: Money Models 7 — Money Models & Offer Stacks (17 min)
lessons.md:
- **A money model = a deliberate series of offers** that minimizes CAC, maximizes GP and collects it within 30 days. (One offer = the unit from $100M Offers; the model sequences them.)
- **The rental-car counter story**: booked online at ~$19/day,walkedout~$400 for 3 days through a smooth chain of offers — (1) "your car isn't available, OK with a bigger truck?" upgrade; (2) late-return option (a fee they invented by defining "late"); (3) "upgrade your insurance?" → declined, but then accepted the **"minimum"** package — naming the cheapest tier "minimum" makes it feel mandatory (many credit cards already include rental cover); (4) prepaid fuel at a small per-gallon premium, but for a whole tank — a fee to avoid a fee; plus damages and late-return penalties. **Lesson: the game-maker invents the rules and fees.** The industry runs thin margins; profit is what keeps the service existing. If 1 in 20 customers is annoyed, don't stop offering to the other 19.
- Study money models of companies that have survived ~30 years in any industry; the models are psychological and **transfer across industries**.
- **Gym Launch's real numbers** ($1k in the bank in Sept 2016 → ~$17M profit 20 months later): **CAC ~$500,30-dayGP~$6,000 (12:1), 12-month GP ~$48,000**. With an "ATM" like that a fixed marketing budget is absurd — spend as much as possible within KPIs.
- Its offer stack: (1) free book/lead magnet/podcast; (2) free strategy call ("leave your card at home", low pressure) → second call; (3) **$16k "fill your gym" intensive** with $1k down + $1k/week terms (affordable because it made them more than that in month one); (4) free supplement-selling training → gyms resell Alex's supplements (price protection so gyms keep the customer, no inventory; the supplement company did ~$1.7M in its first month); (5) **free halfway feedback call** with a "say yes now and keep paying the same, get the next phase and then a lower long-term rate" continuity offer, steering to the ~$3,200/month licensing tier. **Simple scales: as few offers as possible for the most GP in the shortest time.**

lessons.t: Money Models 8 — The 4 Offer Types (12 min)
lessons.md:
- **How he "broke" the gym industry**: his launch ads (e.g. 191 signups in 19 days at $500) vs the industry's "low-barrier offer" model ($19–29 trials with nothing to sell after; ~35% of trials convert) → ~**$600 GP per 10 show-ups**. His model on 10 show-ups: sell to the goal ($500–$2,000 packages), then meals, then supplements (~$85 GP each), then annual commitment, then prepay-for-discount, all inside ~28 days → **~$9,644 GP per 10 show-ups** (~$960 per show-up vs $60). He could outspend competitors ~25:1. Business models and offers aren't IP — it's a **speed game**: rip the value before others copy, then innovate again. Incumbents should have copied him instead of mocking.
- **Downsell flows** for every "no": service (sell to goal → smaller package → free trial with penalty → free trial → free nutrition orientation, where non-buyers still bought ~$300 of supplements); supplements (full bundle → 4-pack + extras → 4-pack → with/without continuity → extras only); meals similar; continuity (goal → small → month-to-month); prepay (whole package → discounted → next month).
- **The 4 prongs** (often built in this sequence, layered over time like coats of paint — don't launch them all at once):
- **Attraction offers** — turn strangers into customers and liquidate CAC.
- **Upsell offers** — maximize profit ("more money").
- **Downsell offers** — maximize conversion (get a yes from people who said no).
- **Continuity offers** — stabilize cash flow (keep them buying).
- Mapped examples: Gym Launch (free content → intensive → supplements → licensing continuity); weight-loss gyms (free promo → challenge / sell-to-goal → supplements → memberships); rental car ($19/day → stack of upsells → rewards program). A model can have several of one type.

lessons.t: Money Models 9 — The Ride-Along Apprenticeship (5 min)
lessons.md:
- Building money models is a pattern-recognition "meta skill" that takes many samples. Teaching works in 3 steps — **document, demonstrate, duplicate** — and in a one-to-many course you have to do the duplicating yourself. What follows is Alex's private "money model journal" of tactics that have already proven themselves ("scratch-off winners"). Each play is covered as: how he learned it, description, examples, key points, summary.
- Mindset: never say "this won't work for my business"; ask **"how could I make this work for my business?"**
- Legal disclaimer: advertising rules vary by place and time; do your own diligence. **When in doubt, give the money back** — getting another customer costs less than repairing a reputation.

lessons.t: Money Models 10 — Attraction Offers Overview (1.5 min)
lessons.md:
- **Attraction offer** = turns ads into customers by offering something free or discounted. Strangers can't judge the value but they understand the price, so bigger discounts mean more demand, and free is the peak.
- The lineup: Win Your Money Back · Free Giveaways · Decoy Offer · Buy X Get Y Free · Pay Less Now or Pay More Later · (video bonus) Free with Consumption.

lessons.t: Money Models 11 — Win Your Money Back (19 min) — "made me more money than any other offer"
lessons.md:
- Origin: in a gym mastermind, an owner called Danny took a hesitant prospect's $500 for 1-on-1 training with a "refund if I lose 20 lb in 8 weeks, and you can use my photos" deal. The before/after photos then brought him ~13 more clients. Alex's tweaks were 6 weeks instead of 8, **run it as the advertised offer**, and **large-group** instead of 1-on-1. That turned it into a "money nuclear bomb", which he later ran in free and paid versions.
- **How it works**: the customer pays up front, you set a goal and give them the path, and if they hit the criteria they get the money back as cash or **store credit**. There are 3 versions:
- **Results**, e.g. lose X lb or get Y clients.
- **Actions**, e.g. attend every session, log progress, take photos, do the homework. Good for subjective outcomes like pain.
- **Both** combined.
- Choose required actions that (a) get the customer results, (b) **advertise your business**, and (c) bring them to your **sales/upsell appointments**.
- It turns onboarding from a cost into a cash-generating, choreographed onboarding. Clients were more invested and got better results; 78% hit their goal.
- **The money comes from the winners, not the losers.** Three weeks into the six, Alex would pitch: "You're down 12 lb, and this is really about a lifestyle change, so let's treat you as if you've already won and credit your deposit toward the long-term program."
- **Fit**: businesses where the customer must do things to succeed (services, some software onboarding). It doesn't fit, say, roofing.
- Examples:
- Rehab "kick the habit in 28 days": attend sessions, post weekly, journal, attend feedback and transformation sessions, pass a test.
- Pain relief: actions only.
- Marketing coaching "5 clients in 5 days": 100 DMs a day plus 5 closes.
- Key points:
- It works with new, current and past customers.
- You **need a back-end offer ~5× the deposit**, so the credit is at most a ~20% discount. If everyone enters through it, raise back-end prices ~20%.
- Alex made it "free" legally by adding an **unconditional service guarantee**: "if at any point you feel you didn't get $500 of value, I'll refund you." He refunded 2 of 4,000+ sales in 5 years. Rule #1 for staying out of trouble: give the money back when asked.
- Sell it as external motivation that builds internal motivation (the "brushing your teeth as a kid" analogy, and "21 days to form a habit, so we double it").
- **Criteria design**: easy to track (ideally already tracked, like phone step counts or photo dates), realistic (copy the fewest common actions of the best performers, then iterate), advertise the business (e.g. 3 workouts a week × 6 weeks × 100 people ≈ 1,800 scripted posts that tag you, plus before/afters), and include the sales appointments.
- **Apply the credit over a long period, never as free months up front.** "3 months free" almost killed Alex's business because people stopped showing up and quit at the first real bill. Instead, $600 credit spread over a $200/month annual plan = $150/month: you got the cash up front and they keep paying (skin in the game).
- **3 built-in appointments**:
- Orientation: before photos, sell supplements.
- Progress check-in: pitch the annual membership.
- Transformation/feedback: after photos, pitch again, and offer prepay to those who already bought.
- **Make everybody a winner** (never mention it up front). At the halfway point, credit the deposit "as if you already won", which is a risk-reduction sale. For people who fail and refuse, "you finished what you started, which was my goal, so I'll credit your whole deposit toward staying."
- Only use it if your normal refund rate is under ~5%. **Never let people stop paying you.**

lessons.t: Money Models 12 — Free Giveaways (24 min)
lessons.md:
- Origin: a business owner gave away a full scholarship to his year-long flagship program. Entrants filled out applications (why me, my pains, my goals), he picked a winner live on a webinar, then **offered everyone else a "partial scholarship"** with its own countdown. He taught online trainers the same structure. The pattern: **grand prize plus participation trophy**.
- Why it's powerful: an audience hoping to win imagines owning the prize, so they're far more receptive. It also builds goodwill. It's legally regulated (charging for entry makes it an illegal lottery), so check local law.
- **Steps**:
- Pick a **grand prize** (ideally the main thing you sell) with a stated value as the price anchor, plus a **promotional offer** (a discount, shorter version or credit toward the grand prize).
- Collect contact info, **eligibility criteria** and application questions (why you, why now, goals), which become ammunition for the sales call and let you score leads. Optionally add promotional actions (bring a friend, join the group, share, review), balancing these against friction.
- Run it on a deadline (**3–7 days**, or until an entry cap based on how many people your team can call).
- Send daily updates that **deliver value and sell the prize** (benefits paired with social proof each day, the Whisper-Tease-Shout pattern), not just "X days left".
- Announce the winner publicly and **deliver the prize**.
- Message everyone else privately: "your application was so strong we want to offer you…". Add a **fresh deadline to claim**, then a **deadline to use**.
- **Sizing**: make the promotional discount ~10–30% of gross margin, but frame it against the full value. Example: $5k value, $2k retail, $1.8k offer reads as $5k of value for $1,800.
- Example offers: a dentist gives away a $6k braces set with a $2k gift card for everyone else; dog food gives a year's supply with a $300 card valid on an annual prepay; a service gives a 1-year package with a $2k voucher; a consultant gives a 16-week program with a "partial" version.
- **If it flops, the prize wasn't grand enough.** A portfolio company selling $15–40k offers gave away $300 event tickets and it bombed. A $50k equipment prize worked.
- **Pro tip — "refer a winner, win too"**: two grand prizes, where whoever referred the winner also wins. This can 2–4× entries, and Skool used it. Prefer your own service as the prize over cash, because the retail-vs-cost arbitrage makes it cheap to give away.
- On the claim call, give two ways to use the credit: first the discount on the grand prize, then the **same % discount** on a smaller back-pocket product (dentist: top teeth only).
- For recurring businesses, spread the discount over the longest term they'll agree to, then auto-bill at the normal rate. Never give "the first 4 months free". If people no-show, switch to personal one-to-one outreach.

lessons.t: Money Models 13 — Decoy Offer (15 min) — "the most flexible attraction offer"
lessons.md:
- Origin: Alex's mentor John (22 tanning salons) put **$5 "5-day VIP" cards** on windshields. Customers didn't know a tan takes multiple sessions ("the turkey talk": you can't cook a turkey faster by turning up the heat). Staff asked what shade they wanted, explained the sessions needed, then offered $25 per session or $19.99/month unlimited with the $5 credited. Most converted to recurring.
- Gym Launch revived it when ads stopped working. The winning test was "**Free 21-Day Transformation**":
- Decoy: 1 workout a week plus an at-home nutrition course.
- Premium: unlimited workouts, personalized nutrition, grocery lists and a result guarantee.
- **70–80% should take the premium.** Advertise the result, not the vehicle, so you're free to choose the vehicle and price in the sale. You must still honestly deliver the free version promised in the ad.
- **Steps**:
- Advertise a lesser, simpler or older version of your offer as the decoy, free or discounted (e.g. $21).
- When leads engage, present **both side by side**, emphasizing the premium (more features, bonuses, guarantees).
- Everyone closes on one or the other (an assumed close).
- To build the decoy, strip out the features that cost you most, depersonalize it, or offer an older version.
- Examples:
- Lemonade: warm powdered vs organic, cold, delivered.
- Float spa: 1 float a month plus DIY vs 2 a week plus consulting and a guarantee.
- Gym: online group plus general plan vs unlimited plus personalized plus guarantee.
- **Contrast must be huge**: if many people take the decoy, it's too good or the premium is too weak.
- Discounted decoys get better show rates than free ones.
- **Selling script**:
- Ask the sorting question first: "Are you here for free stuff or lasting results?" "Results" gives you permission to present the premium first.
- If they say yes to the premium, stop talking and close.
- If they ask for free, present the decoy and immediately contrast with "and…" (don't pause for a yes).
- Then ask which they'd prefer, or which will get them to the goal faster.
- Deliver it **matter-of-fact, almost bored**: "this is what everyone does; got your ID and card?" Most people don't remember exactly what they opted in for.
- **Optional surprise**: if someone takes the decoy, throw in a low-cost premium feature for free (e.g. a nutrition consult, which is where you sell supplements). This builds goodwill and sets up the later upsell.

lessons.t: Money Models 14 — Buy X Get Y Free (13 min)
lessons.md:
- Ethics reminder: making more offers isn't unethical; **lying** is (about their fit or about what you'll deliver). Good selling is education. A test: would you recommend the same purchase to your mother if she knew everything you know?
- Origin: Nashville's "Boot Factory", with its buy-one-get-two-free sign. Ten years later Alex realized each pair was priced ~$600 (about 3 × a fair $200), so the free pairs were baked in. Bachelorette parties piled in and the store kept expanding.
- **Principle**: free gets more attention than a discount. Selling multiple units lets you turn a discount into a "free" offer. 3 shirts at $10 each is weak; "buy 1 for $30, get 2 free" is the same economics and far stronger. Adding a real discount: 3 for $20 = "buy 1 for $20, get 2 free".
- **More free than paid wins**: buy 1 get 2 > buy 2 get 1. For 18 months at $1,800, "buy 6 get 12 free" > "buy 9 get 9" > "buy 12 get 6", all at the same price.
- The free item can differ from the paid one ("buy a shirt, get 3 pairs of socks free" may beat "a shirt free"). Test it.
- **Uses**:
- **Grand openings** ("buy 6 months, get 6 free", with full-price prepayments and possibly a small high-margin extra like text access to justify a higher price).
- **Fast cash** from existing customers to fund equipment instead of debt.
- **Extending duration**: if customers usually stay 3 months, "buy 2 get 2" keeps them 4 (~33% more money).
- One-shot businesses (tourists): pack as much as possible into the first sale.
- Raise prices before giving things away so you protect margin.
- **Cautions**:
- Only do this if you can manage money (put prepaid cash in a separate account and draw it monthly).
- Never do it to keep a dying business alive.
- **Cap prepay at ~10% of a recurring base**, a psychological rather than mathematical rule.
- **Prepaid customers are your best buyers**: they forget they paid, so they buy the most add-ons (seminars, specialty camps). Keep selling to them.

lessons.t: Money Models 15 — Pay Less Now or Pay More Later (14 min)
lessons.md:
- Origin: a speed-reading webinar. "$0 today, billed $300 after the 3-hour training unless your reading speed didn't double (attendance required)". The next page offered "**or pay $97 now and get the recordings**". During the session he tested everyone at the start and halfway, helped live those who weren't improving, then pitched an 8-week intensive at the end.
- **Structure**:
- **Pay later**: full price, delayed, with a **conditional satisfaction guarantee**. You can advertise it as free, you get the **card on file**, and show rates soar.
- **Pay now**: ~20–50% off (up to ~⅔) plus bonuses, presented **right after** they accept the pay-later option ("oh, I forgot to ask, want to save $200?").
- **Upsell** later.
- Balance the split so pay-now cash covers CAC and as many people as possible take the 3×-priced pay-later. Pay-later money still lands inside 30 days, so it counts toward CFA.
- People agree to pay more later, and a guaranteed-result price can be higher.
- Examples:
- Real-estate 3-day workshop: $0 now / $500 later vs $299 now plus recordings, a 1-on-1 expert call and printed materials, then a $30k six-month program.
- Clothing: 14-day try-before-you-buy at $149, or $97 now plus an accessory, then a subscription.
- Lawn care: $600 after the job or $369 now plus a treatment, then a $199/month plan, with the rep presenting both on site.
- Subscriptions: free trial then $400/month, or "pay $300 today, skip the trial and lock in $300/month for life".
- **Keys**:
- Promise a clear **yes/no, measurable** result you can deliver within the time frame (measure before and during).
- Make the guarantee conditional on value-getting actions (attendance, data).
- Stack pay-now bonuses.
- **Tuning**: if too many choose pay later, sweeten pay now, and vice versa. **Expect ~10% of pay-later people to cancel.** More than that means you over-promised, the conditions are too loose, the price is too high or you're selling to the wrong people. Attend to people who aren't getting results during the session to prevent cancellations.
- **Hint at the next offer early**: "everyone asks which supplements to buy, we'll get to that, but first…". This implies that everyone buys, without pitching.

lessons.t: Money Models 16 — Free with Consumption (video-only bonus, 25 min)
lessons.md:
- Origin: at an event where pitching was banned, a speaker gave a full presentation and then said "if you want more, go over there". Alex wanted to buy, and that was his first webinar. In this offer you give away a **selling tool that also delivers real value** (a 20-minute video, PDF, audio, live event, workshop, or a 1–5-day challenge). It's the most skill-heavy play and payback can stretch past 30 days.
- It **reverse-engineers trust**: the best proof they'll get value after paying is getting value before paying. Education is the core of marketing. Think "FAQs on steroids" that systematically break the prospect's false beliefs, with embedded CTAs.
- **"The bigger the plane, the longer the runway"**: the consumption needed scales with price relative to buying power (a $20 product can sell from a 7-second ad; timeshares need a 7-day trip). Marketing and sales are one continuum; this "microwaves" the prospect.
- Formats and benchmarks:
- Chiro "neuropathy dinners": ~90 minutes of presentation over dinner sells a $50–100 consult (~25% of the room), and ~⅓ of those buy a $5–10k program, so ~10% of attendees overall.
- 3–5-day challenges and summits: **give, give, give, pitch, re-pitch with proof** (Q&A, case studies, re-stack). Virtual events convert **~2–5% of opt-ins** (higher for niche or warm audiences).
- **Webinars**: a 90-minute compression (origin story, obstacles, ~45–60 minutes of value, ~30 minutes of pitch and stack), converting ~10% of live attendees.
- **Strategy calls** ("I won't ask for your card on this call"): a genuinely useful qualification call, then hand off to an edified closer. Aim for ≥25% to book the sales call.
- Sample 5-day arc:
- Our story, why it's like yours, why we can help, the perspective shift.
- Their fear about their own ability.
- The external obstacle.
- Introduce the core offer.
- Pitch, then re-pitch with Q&A and proof.
- **Beginner version (simplest way to sell)**: one-on-one, "I'll spend 5 one-hour sessions with you to get [goal]".
- Day 1: get permission to make an offer at the end, learn their goals, obstacles and past pain (a CLOSER-style flow).
- Middle sessions: break the beliefs one-on-one.
- End: ask for referrals, then present the offer, or ask "what would working with me for $3k/year look like to you?"
- Alex's first business: clients donated $500–1,000 to a charity of their choice for 12 weekly sessions, then he pitched. Lesson learned: pitch halfway, and it could have been 6 weeks.
- Headline examples: 5-day "find your perfect product", "find your agency niche", plateau buster, get unstuck.
- **The 3 beliefs every sale must break**:
- **Circumstances** ("no money/time" really means not resourceful or not prioritizing; point the finger back at yourself).
- **Other people** (spouse, partner, kids: ask for support, not permission, and reframe it as helping them).
- **Self** ("I can't, I'm afraid": frame the decision as already made long ago, with today as the first action).
- **Belief-breaking formula**: what you believed → why it's wrong → what's right → why it's right → proof. **Teach concepts, not tactics** (everyone values concepts; only doers value tactics).
- Free consumption pieces can be inserted anywhere in a sales process (a video before call 1, between calls). Use as much friction as needed, no more. Losing the wrong people is good.

lessons.t: Money Models 17 — Upsell Offers Overview (5 min)
lessons.md:
- An upsell is simply **whatever you offer next**. Every solved problem reveals another one, and that new problem is what you sell against. Upsells often make up the **majority of profit** even when the front end sells more units, so it makes sense to accept a weak front-end margin in exchange for 10× the customers.
- Burger example: a $2 burger with $1.75 of cost leaves $0.25 profit. Add fries, a soda and "supersize it?" and gross profit per sale rises roughly 8×. Work out what your "fries and Coke" are, or a competitor will.
- **Why upsells fail or feel cringy**:
- **Wrong thing**: it doesn't relate to their problem.
- **Wrong time**: the problem isn't felt yet, or it has just been satisfied.
- **Wrong way**: they don't believe you.
- What to sell next: **more** (quantity), **better** (quality) or **new** (complementary).
- The plays covered: Classic, Menu, Anchor, Rollover. All of them can also work as front ends.

lessons.t: Money Models 18 — Classic Upsell: "You can't have X without Y" (13 min)
lessons.md:
- **The fur-coat summer job.** A 4th-generation furrier stored about 7,000 coats over summer at ~$200 each, roughly $1.4M. He drew people in with **free earmuffs**, then offered $30 storage and conditioning (earmuffs included) with the line **"You don't want anything else, do you?"** That is the **no-sale sale**: people are conditioned to say "no" to salesmen, so phrase it so that "no" means "just that, thanks", which is a yes to the thing already offered.
- **The gym rescue offer.** When someone declined all services, Alex offered a free at-home program on a thumb drive plus a free nutrition consult in a couple of days. At the consult those people bought supplements at the **same close rate** as members but a **higher ticket** (~$300vs~$200). They wanted a magic pill rather than the work, so offer the problem's solution in the form they want.
- **Storage-unit owner story: "how much does a free month of storage cost?" Answer: ~$127.** The $127 comes from add-ons:
- The only lock that fits (~$47)
- Boxes and hand-truck rental
- Insurance upgrade, about $10/month for far more cover at ~90% margin
- Bigger units, because "eyes are bigger than stomachs"

If customers have to buy something anyway, the only question is whether they buy it from you. - **Description**: give thing A free (or cheap) and monetize it through the natural companion B. - Examples: - Lemonade: lemonade ice cubes, a steel to-go mug with a charity tie-in, discounted refills - Physical therapy: 4 free treatments, then orthotics, bands, braces, tape - Education or community: free, as long as they keep using your software (Skool's model) - Weight-loss chain: services for ~$5/month,then~$5k of supplements on day 2. Alex paid their top supplement seller **$500/hour for 2 hours** to teach him everything; it "made me millions". Pay skilled operators for their know-how, not just info-sellers. - **Key points**: - If you advertise something as free, you must deliver it free. - Keep it cheap for you. - Make the upsell the next **natural, near-required** item (like the rental car's "minimum" package), without making it mandatory. - Make it seamless. - Prefer low operational drag. - **Benchmark: 80%+ take rate.** At around 30% the upsell isn't assumed or "goes-with" enough. - It also works internally on existing customers, and it's easy even for weak salespeople.

lessons.t: Money Models 19 — Menu Upsell (Alex's favourite, 19 min)
lessons.md:
- **Four steps: Unsell → Prescribe → A/B → Card on file.** Each step was learned separately:
- **A/B + card on file**: 19 failed consults in a row, then an exhausted Alex just asked "vanilla or chocolate?", gave his own preference, then said "use the card ending in 46?" She bought, and he closed the rest of the day without describing a single product.
- **Prescription**: a client asked so many questions that he wrote out exact dosing and timing. The next client asked for "what you did for her", so he just said "you'll need 2 of these, 1 of these…", went to card on file, and she bought everything. Detailed post-purchase instructions **assume the sale**.
- **Unsell**: after running out of stock, he told a client which items to get elsewhere ("not as good, but it'll get you through") and then prescribed the rest. That was suspiciously easy, so he started deliberately listing items most people don't need (weight gainer and test booster for mostly-female clients) and **crossing them out**. He even "gave away" low-margin fish oil to sell the high-margin fat burner. Telling people what they don't need makes them believe what you say they do need.
- **Steps in practice**:
- **Unsell**: cross out what they don't need.
- **Prescribe**: explain how it fits with what they already bought, and personalize when, how much and what if, as though it's already purchased.
- **A/B**: "which do you prefer?" instead of yes/no. Anything can be A/B: flavour, start date, which coach, morning or evening, DM or phone support. Add a **nudge** ("most people/big dogs like beef"), steering toward higher margin or whatever stock is high.
- **Card on file**: removes the second decision of reaching for a wallet. It's also the fastest close.
- Examples:
- Massage: unsell lymphatic massage, prescribe heat, trigger points, stretches, then before work or on the way home, then card.
- Dog food: unsell puppy bag and vitamins, prescribe joint chews and heartworm wafer, book next month, chicken or beef, card.
- Digital: "you don't need all 8 courses…"
- **Pro tips**:
- If you're out of stock or at capacity, take payment and deliver later. Customers mind broken expectations much more than delay: say 7 days and deliver in 4.
- Staff love unselling ("homie hookups") and it's even more believable coming from an employee. Script it.
- **The Economist decoy**: digital at $59 vs digital + print at $125 → most bought digital only. Adding print-only at $125 made digital + print the obvious deal. With two products, offer A, B, and **A+B priced at the more expensive of A or B**.

lessons.t: Money Models 20 — Anchor Upsell (14 min)
lessons.md:
- **Story**: Alex budgeted ~$500 for his first business suit. The tailor (a friend's contact, 3rd generation) put him in a $16,000 suit first. Alex went pale, the tailor asked "do you care much about the brand?", and swapped him into a near-identical $2,200 suit. Alex walked out spending ~$2.5–3k with shirts and socks, **5–6× his budget**. Rory Sutherland's Rolls-Royce example makes the same point: they show at jet and yacht shows, not car shows, because a $400k car feels cheap after declining a $50M jet.
- **How it works**:
- Present a premium version **5–10× the price** first. It must be an order of magnitude more, not +20%.
- **Get the gasp.** No gasp means it wasn't high enough or you didn't present it sincerely.
- **Come to the rescue**: "Do you care about [secondary feature]?"
- Present the main offer with the **same primary features**, differing only in secondary ones, so their price-to-value reasoning carries over and it feels like an 80–90% discount.
- Ask how they'd like to pay.
- **Bonus economics**: some people buy the anchor anyway. If 1 in 10 buys something priced 10× higher, you double the business; 1 in 5 buying a $16ksuitadds~$3k to every average sale. Menu upsells are elegant and suit high volume; anchors are brute force and suit fewer, bigger buyers.
- "The only thing worse than offering $1,000 to someone with a $100 budget is offering $100 to someone with a $1,000 budget." **Always have a premium offer ready.**
- Examples:
- Lawn care: $1,000/week with the owner's cell, premium mulch, natural pest control, vs $200/week with the foreman's number and standard inputs. Previously, $200 quoted straight up got haggled down to $99–150.
- Painting: premium packaging, 20-year insurance and gift wrap at $1,000 vs standard at $200.
- Newsletter: archive + 24-hour early access at $199/month vs new issues only at $19/month, where you might previously have competed at $7.
- **Key points**:
- **Treat the anchor seriously.** Let them genuinely consider it so their brain justifies the value.
- Only build an anchor you're willing to deliver; more than 1 in 10 may buy it.
- Staff often rush the anchor because they "sell from their own wallet". Train against that. You sell what's easy for you and hard for them.
- If they don't gasp, **close the whale** and keep adding.

lessons.t: Money Models 21 — Rollover Upsell (Alex's most-used, 14 min)
lessons.md:
- **Origin**: crediting Win-Your-Money-Back winnings as months of free service up front ($600 = 4 free months) hurt cash flow and engagement. A gym-owner friend in Vegas kept 70%+ paying by **crediting the winnings toward a year-long plan**.
- **Definition**: credit some or all of a previous purchase toward the next, bigger offer. Decide **who / what / how**.
- **Who**:
- **Win-back**: customers gone 6+ months. Subject line "I owe you money", then credit toward a new plan.
- **Upset customers**: a do-over instead of a refund. "That's on me; I'll credit what you paid toward what I should have sold you."
- **Competitors' upset customers**: work through their 1-star reviews and credit what they spent elsewhere, or the remaining months on their contract, toward a longer agreement with you. Their biggest hater becomes your ambassador.
- **Current customers**: roll a just-bought block into a 12-month membership immediately.
- **What**: more, better or new, ideally **≥4–5× the credit** so the discount is at most ~20–25%.
- **How**: apply it all up front or spread it over time. You can invent a fee to waive. You don't have to credit everything: for long-tenure customers, credit the last purchase or the last 6 months.
- Examples:
- Chiropractor win-back: "I wanted to give you your money back… a $500 credit toward staying pain-free for good."
- Dentist: a $200 cleaning credited toward a whitening package.
- Alex recorded ~200 personalized videos to past customers offering ~$4k credits.
- **Make it one-time-only** ("take it now or pay full price later").
- **The gift-card play** (holidays, Black Friday):
- Sell $200 gift cards for $20, max 2 per person, **only usable by someone else**.
- Ask who it's for and get an intro.
- Roll the card into a main offer priced ≥5× the card (e.g. $1k–2k+), optionally with a high-margin add-on to justify it.
- Customers effectively pay you to refer hot leads, and unused cards are pure cash.

lessons.t: Money Models 22 — Downsell Offers Overview (5 min)
lessons.md:
- A downsell is what you offer after a "no". Change **how they pay** (now vs later, amount over time) or **what they get** (quality, quantity, something different).
- **Don't**: a car salesman dropped the same $5k insurance step by step to $400. The buyer stopped trusting him and doubted the car price too. Lowering the price of the same thing destroys trust, for that buyer and everyone they tell. **Offer something different for less, never the same thing for less.**
- **Rules**:
- They said no to this offer, not to every offer. Use it to find out what they want.
- Downsells are **trades**: if you give something, get something back.
- Personalize, don't pressure.
- It's "100 ways to offer what you already have."
- Dropping the price is discounting, not downselling. A payment plan is fine.
- The plays covered: payment plans (how they pay), trial with penalty (how they pay), feature downsells (what they get). They can sit anywhere in the model.

lessons.t: Money Models 23 — Payment Plan Downsells (17 min)
lessons.md:
- **Origin**: in month one, with one month's rent left, a prospect said no. Alex asked about half down, then a third down, and finally settled on $0 today with the full amount charged on her payday, the 1st. Rent was due on the 5th.
- People reject what something costs **today**, not overall. Payment plans get the most buyers at the highest price, but they're a gamble: you lose if people cancel early, or if people who would have paid in full switch to plans and then cancel.
- **The 7-step sequence**:
- **Reward paying in full rather than punishing payment plans.** Quote the full payment-plan price first (e.g. $12k), then "want to save some money? Prepay $10k." It also doubles as a price test: if people keep saying yes at $12k, nudge the price up.
- **Financing**:
- Third-party financing: typically +~35% revenue.
- **The credit-card reframe**: "Would you rather I choose your payment terms or you choose?" "Me." "Great, use your credit card." The alternative is your shorter in-house plan.
- **Layaway**: pay it off before receiving it. Incentives align because they want to pay fast. With Alan's ~$20k white-label onboarding, agency owners proposed $800 every two weeks; once told they could only fly out when paid off, they paid in full within a month.
- **Half now, half on the next paycheck or cash inflow.** If not: "What's the most you can put down today?" Bill on paycheck dates (every 2 weeks), so 3 payments land in 30 days.
- **Temperature check**: "1–10, how badly do you want this?" At 8 or above, keep working the payment plans. At 7 or below, ask "why not a 10?" and pivot to a **feature downsell**.
- **Thirds**: now plus the next two paychecks or months.
- **Spread evenly**, still front-loaded where possible (pay over 3 months for 6 months of service). Gym Launch billed weekly over its 16 weeks.
- **Free trial** (next lesson).
- **Seesaw alternative** (more flexible, suits owner-operators; step-downs suit larger teams and finance departments): "Would you rather have giant monthly payments or tiny ones?" → tiny → "normally X; prepay today and you get a big discount and zero monthly payments" → if not, "the more you put down, the lower your monthly payment."
- **Built-in upsell**: extend the pay-in-full discount window ~30 days and remind them at weeks 2–3. Many prepay once they trust you.
- Align billing with paychecks to cut declines.
- Health check: close rate should rise. If the number of pay-in-full buyers falls, you have a problem.
- **Pay sales reps on cash collected today.** Save any back-end commission for the people who keep customers paying.
- For recurring businesses: quote the annual price (e.g. $36k), offer a prepay price ($30k), otherwise $3k/month.

lessons.t: Money Models 24 — Trial with Penalty (17 min)
lessons.md:
- **Origin**: Leila picked an HR platform because it charged $500 and **rebated it if she attended 2–3 onboarding sessions**. She learned it, and they kept her for years.
- **Concept**: the mirror image of Win Your Money Back. The trial is free **as long as they meet the terms**; they only pay if they don't. Fees are tied to the same 4 criteria: actions that get results, attending sales consults, advertising your business, and tracking. **Weight the fees** by importance. For example, if a Win-Your-Money-Back deposit would be $500 across 10 tasks, charge $50 per task, or $100–150 for a consult vs $25 for minor items.
- **Use it last, as a downsell** (Alex doesn't advertise it). Close 3/10 on the main offer, downsell 4 more to the trial, upsell 3 of those, and you've doubled customers. Sales rule: **everyone who's qualified buys something.**
- **Selling steps**:
- "That's a pickle… how about we get you started for free?" → **ask for their ID**, which gets the wallet out.
- **Fill in the contract yourself** while making small talk, hold the ID, then "I'll trade you for whichever card you want to use," and copy the card number yourself. If they ask why a card for a free trial: "**It's just to complete your account profile… it's how we've always done it.**"
- **Sell staying and paying first**: "If this gets you the result, will you stay long-term? You won't hit the long-term goal in the trial, but you'll build the habits." If they won't commit, don't give the trial. This gives you the moral high ground.
- **Explain the fees only after you have the card**: "We do our part, you do yours… if you miss things your results suffer, so a small ding keeps you on track… it's the best way to get you results and keep it free, the best of both worlds." Have them **initial each fee**. Present the required check-ins as nutrition, progress and transformation, which are really sales consults.
- **Upselling out of a trial**:
- **They like it**: pitch the longer or higher tier at the mid or end meeting.
- **They hate it**: "What would you have liked different? You're right, I'm angry at myself," then offer the higher-level fit. About half buy.
- **They didn't use it**: offer to **waive the fees if they get back on track**. Alex prefers not to bill non-starters because of the 1-star risk, but billing is justified after a second miss.
- **Tuning**:
- Nobody takes the trial: lower the requirements.
- People take it but don't follow through: emphasize why the fees exist and that meetings are mandatory.
- People don't stay on: emphasize "stay and pay" up front.
- Let people make up for goofs.
- Just call it a "trial — we do it a special way."
- **When to use which**: Pay Less Now / Pay More Later as the downsell for **physical or one-time** products; Trial with Penalty for **recurring** ones where the customer must do work. If a free trial with a card is awkward, use $1 or a small paid first month. Rebates (pay up front, get it back for doing X) suit smaller-scope offers. Prefer small per-item dings over one big fee.

lessons.t: Money Models 25 — Feature Downsells (16 min)
lessons.md:
- **Origin.** A friend tripled his close rate, from about 25% to about 75%, without discounts or payment plans. When people balked at his $4k offer, he offered it for less with **the guarantee removed**. Seeing the guarantee's value next to the price gap, many people re-sold themselves on the full offer (about 35 of 100 bought full price and about 40 took the downsell).
- **Mechanics.** Take something away, lower the price, and ask "how about now?" Every feature has a price and a value. Customers weigh the money saved against the value lost.
- **Remove something valuable and drop the price a little.** People re-upsell themselves.
- **Remove things they don't care about and drop the price a lot.** More people take the downsell.
- Alex's standard sequence:
- Cut something valuable (e.g. the guarantee) for a small discount, which pushes them to reconsider the original.
- Then restore it, cut low-value features and take a big discount, so they find the best deal.
- **Levers you can turn down (or up, for premium tiers):**
- Quantity: fewer units, sessions or months.
- Product quality: older model, cheaper materials (vinyl instead of leather).
- Service quality:
- Availability: set hours vs anytime, days of the week, minutes per call, one location vs all.
- Rescheduling fees.
- Response speed and delivery speed.
- Ratio: 1:1 vs group vs "many experts on you".
- Channel: text, chat or video.
- Who delivers: owner, senior or junior.
- Live vs recorded, in person vs remote.
- DIY, done-with-you or done-for-you.
- Expiration.
- Personalization.
- Guarantee: length, coverage, conditional or unconditional.
- Remove a whole component, e.g. drop calls and keep chat and email.
- **Done-for-you → DIY**: chiropractic → at-home tools; house painting → paint plus a rented sprayer; acquisition.com partnership → a workshop.
- **Rules:**
- Never negotiate on price. Stay a helpful guide: "let's find what works for you." That gives you unlimited shots on goal.
- Learn which features customers value most, then standardize the order you remove them in.
- Name the tiers (first, business, economy). Call the cheapest one "**minimum**". If they reject everything: "so nothing more than the minimum package, then?"
- **Temperature check after two refusals** ("1–10, how badly?"). At 8 or above, the features fit but the price doesn't, so move to **payment-plan downsells**. After each step ask "**Deal? Fair enough?**", which uses reciprocity. (Alex's podcast episode 202 covers the exact tonality.)
- If they buy nothing, offer a **free orientation**, then sell a DIY product there.
- **Pro tip: downsell current customers before they churn.** One portfolio company found its second-highest-LTV segment was mid-priced customers who had been proactively moved to a cheaper plan matching what they actually used ("you only use 4 of 6 features"). Churn almost vanished because they trusted the company.
- **Only legitimate price cut without changing what they get: change what they give you (barter).** "$400 instead of $500 if you leave reviews, give testimonials, post daily and introduce two friends now." This also protects you when others ask why Susan paid less.

lessons.t: Money Models 26 — Continuity Offers Overview (16 min)
lessons.md:
- Continuity means ongoing value for ongoing payments until they cancel. You sell once and get paid repeatedly. Example: $1,000 one-time to 100 people with 10 buying = $10k now. At $50/month, 40 buy, and over 20 months that's $2k now plus $40k over time, **with 4× the customers to upsell later**. The downside is less cash now, which is why it comes last, after attraction, upsell and downsell cash.
- **Downsell the upsell.** Sell a short, higher-priced front program, then offer the long-term continuity at a **lower weekly price with more value** (e.g. $600 for 6 weeks → $200/month membership with perks). Script: "Enjoyed it so far? Mind if I show you a way to save a bit and get a lot more?" People think about the monthly payment more than the term. Gym Launch moved clients to 3-year contracts with lower monthly payments.
- **Back-of-napkin LTV:** lifetime revenue = price ÷ monthly churn; × gross margin = LTGP. Example: $100, 80% margin, 10% churn → $1,000 revenue → $800 LTGP. Going from 10% to 3% churn gives $3,333, more than 3× (not a "7%" change). Even low-value subscriptions usually last about 3 months, so adding a subscription option for a one-time product can roughly triple that customer's value. **Conquer churn.**
- **Big head, long tail** (learned from John the tanning-salon owner, who said you can shear a sheep for life but skin it only once). He offered $100 down plus $10/month or $19.99/month, and people called before their cards expired to keep the $10 rate. A big upfront payment plus a low monthly rate gives very low churn (sunk cost) and helps fund acquisition.
- **Why info and education businesses churn: price-to-value mismatch.** Information loses value once it's learned. **Split one-time value from consumable value.** Charge one-time or annual for the system (e.g. Gym Launch's sales system) and run continuity on what's genuinely new each month (consultant calls, new plays, new ads). Annual plans also give you time to find the next problem to solve.
- **Enterprise value.** Recurring and predictable revenue gets about 8–15× vs about 4× for transactional (e.g. the same $3M EBITDA is worth $12M vs $24–45M). Recurring (Netflix) and reoccurring (Coca-Cola, his favourite sauce bought for 4 years) both count if you can show them. You also sleep well when the month's bills are covered on the 1st.

lessons.t: Money Models 27 — Continuity Bonus Offers (21 min)
lessons.md:
- **Origins.**
- An ad: "I'm giving away all my courses free" (about $24k value) with a 30-day trial of a $399/month newsletter. The thank-you page offered "or pay today and lock in a lower monthly rate for life, plus the back issues".
- A gym owner who crushed everyone's numbers raised the price of his challenge, then **gave the challenge free to anyone who joined as a member**. He closed 70–80% of walk-ins at full membership price.
- **Definition:** give an awesome bonus if they sign up today, **worth more than the first continuity payment**. Bonuses add good stuff; discounts remove bad stuff; both increase starts. Add urgency (today only).
- **Order:** big-cash attraction, upsells and downsells first (already profitable), then a soft continuity pitch with bonuses, then **offer a prepay discount to new members** to pull more cash forward.
- Examples:
- Dog food: every toy they make ($800 value) free with $59/month food, plus a new toy monthly.
- Service: a $1k accelerator free with a $100/month membership, plus VIP perks.
- Newsletter: 40 back issues free with $3.99/month after a trial, or lock in $2.99 for life plus print copies.
- **Key points:**
- **Advertise the bonus, not the membership.**
- Keep bonuses related to the core offer. A free t-shirt for tech services attracts the wrong people.
- Use things you already have and do (back issues, onboarding repackaged as a "program").
- Cross physical and digital (gloves with a digital membership, livestreams with a gym).
- Use believable value anchors; past real prices with receipts are best.
- **Status titles** (silver, gold, diamond) placed just after common churn points, with growing intervals like game levels. One friend's customers introduced themselves by title.
- Sell the bonus seriously first, like an anchor, then ask "want to know how to get it free?" and stack the member perks with dollar values.
- **Pricing data from Alex's brick-and-mortar fitness tests** (standalone bonus price vs first month of continuity plus bonus):
- About 1.33× → about 50/50.
- About 1.66× → about 60% choose continuity.
- About 2× → about 70%.
- About 2.3× → about 80%.
- About 2.66–3× → about 90%.

People pay about a 33% premium to avoid being on continuity. Price the standalone according to how much upfront cash you need. - **Bulk prepay upsell for members.** If just 1 in 8 takes "buy 5 months, get 1 free", 30-day profit rises about 50%. Bigger free portions convert more. - You can tie the bonus to a 3/6/12-month commitment (fewer takers, but locked-in terms). If unsure, start simple: standalone bonus or month-to-month.

lessons.t: Money Models 28 — Continuity Discount Offers (21 min)
lessons.md:
- **Story:** Alex's neighbour in Austin maxed out his credit cards to give apartment buildings **a year of trash service free for signing 5 years**. He won market share, sold to a national company and bought a Ferrari. It worked, but the cash flow was brutal.
- **Definition:** give time free or discounted if they commit to more. Seen in pools, gyms, landscaping, storage, leases. You need to decide **how to apply the discount** and **the cancellation policy**.
- **4 ways to apply it:**
- **Up front**, pushing the term out (3 free + 12 paid). Works where contracts can be enforced or there's collateral (phones, storage, real estate, cars). Skip it if churn is high. It delays cash. **Never make it 3 + 9 instead of 3 + 12**; that's 33% less money.
- **At the end**, earned by paying all 12 on time. This encourages on-time payment.
- **Spread over the term**: $600 of credit over 12 months at $200 = $150/month, advertised as "3 months free / $600 off". Full price after the term.
- **Hybrid**: collect **first + last month** (or an onboarding fee) up front, then the free months, then the paid term. This liquidates CAC and proves the card works.
- Display the same discount 4 ways: "3 months free", "$3,000 off", "25% off", or a comparison.
- **Highest value per word in the course:**
- **Bill every 4 weeks, not monthly.** That's 13 billing cycles a year, about 8.3% more revenue with no difference in take rates. Quote the price weekly but bill every 4 weeks (weekly billing creates admin pain). At a 20% net margin that's roughly +40% profit.
- **Add a 3% processing fee.** It goes straight to profit, and he's never seen it cost a sale. Then **waive it in exchange for a second form of payment**, ideally **ACH** (bank accounts change far less often than cards, rarely decline and cost less to process). Lost cards and declines cause much of churn, so cutting involuntary churn more than repays the waived 3%.
- **Gift-card version:** mail the free months as a card usable after the first 3 payments, or giftable to a friend. Outcomes: they redeem it later, it becomes a free referral, or they forget it and you got a full-price signup.
- **Lifetime discount at the most common churn point** (e.g. Amazon Subscribe & Save: 5% off, rising to 15% after 5 deliveries). Advertise it up front and **remind them as it approaches** ("2 months to your new lower rate").
- **Cancellation options:**
- Cancel any time during the trial: more sales, lower stick.
- No cancellations: only works with good customers.
- Pro-rated repayment of savings.
- **One-time breakup fee** (simplest, and a negotiating chip). Alex's favourite is a fee **equal to the discount they received**.
- **Make cancelling easy and clear.** Unhappy customers with nowhere to complain inside your business complain publicly. Offer "**fee or feedback**": waive the fee if they sit down for an exit interview. Let them vent, get angrier about the problem than they are, own it, then offer a rollover do-over into the right tier.
- Front-loaded discounts convert more but churn more; back-loaded convert less but churn less; spreading balances cash and value.

lessons.t: Money Models 29 — Waived Fee Offer (10 min)
lessons.md:
- **Origin:** a friend running a lifestyle consulting business (about $5M/year, no staff, "I don't lose anyone") offered "$25k to start then $4k month-to-month, **or $4k/month with the fee waived if you commit to a year**." Nearly everyone committed and initialled that leaving early triggers the $25k onboarding fee. When someone called to quit: "No worries, just wire the onboarding fee." Most stayed, which also carried them through the emotional ups and downs.
- **Structure:**
- Set the month-to-month starter fee at **3–5× the monthly rate**.
- **Waive it for a commitment of 6+ months (ideally 12+)**.
- If they cancel early, they owe the fee.
- **Once the term is complete, the fee disappears.** That's what makes it fair.
- After a few months, paying the fee costs about the same as staying, so it carries customers past the usual churn point.
- **Justification:** onboarding a new customer costs more than serving an existing one, so short-term flexibility means they cover their setup cost, and commitment means you cover it. Possible names: onboarding, activation, enrollment, setup, initiation fee.
- **Variables:** commitment length, committed rate, month-to-month rate, fee size. A smaller fee (1.5–3×) pushes more people to month-to-month (more cash up front); a larger fee pushes more to commit. Variant: a higher month-to-month rate with the savings difference billed on cancellation.
- **Watch out:** if more than about 5% try to cancel early, fix the product. This should nudge people, not handcuff them to something they hate. Works best for long-horizon results (SEO, investing, weight loss).
- Advanced trick: on early cancellation, donate the fee to **a cause the customer dislikes**.

lessons.t: Money Models 30 — Make Your Own Money Model (9 min)
lessons.md:
- The duplicate step is yours. Beginners should pick one play. More advanced people can weave plays together in any order (attraction offers as upsells, continuity as a front end; no rules as long as it's legal).
- **Alex's real models:**
- **Fitness gyms:**
- Front end: Win Your Money Back.
- Upsells: Buy X Get Y Free (prepay), then a continuity bonus.
- If no: Trial with Penalty downsell, then a menu upsell on supplements, then a rollover upsell on the back end.
- **Gym Launch:**
- Front end: decoy offer / free-with-consumption strategy call.
- Then a classic upsell, then a menu upsell into "Gym Legacy" service levels (e.g. ads only vs sales training).
- If no: payment plan, feature downsell, free trial.
- **Newsletter + consulting:**
- Front end: free-trial attraction.
- Cash flow from pay-now (skip the trial, get back issues plus a lifetime lower rate).
- Then consulting upsells.
- Alex would add Buy X Get Y Free on top of continuity, but only if average tenure is short (e.g. about 3 months). With a 2-year tenure it would lose money.
- **Steps:** (1) pick an attraction offer; (2) an upsell (menu/anchor/rollover…); (3) a downsell flow (payment plan → feature → trial); (4) a continuity offer. Result: cash back in 30 days, more customers, more money.
- **Notes:**
- **Perfect one at a time.** Adding several at once will break the business.
- Start at a lower price, get yeses, then raise prices in stages. The payment-plan-first quote doubles as a price test.
- **"Simple scales, fancy fails."** Use the fewest offers needed to cover CAC within 30 days. Once acquisition isn't the bottleneck, the job is done.
- **Affiliate products can fill gaps** (e.g. run Buy X Get Y Free on someone else's product, with no operational load).
- Any attraction offer can become continuity automatically by adding a renewal clause.

lessons.t: Money Models 31 — 10 Years in 10 Minutes (recap, 9 min)
lessons.md:
- The trilogy: Offers (what to sell, so good people feel stupid saying no), Leads (how to find people: advertise), Money Models (how to get them to buy).
- A **good** model makes more profit from one customer than it costs to get and serve them within 30 days. A **$100M** model makes more profit from one customer than it costs to get and serve many customers within 30 days, which removes cash as a limit. Results Alex cites: Alan, $0 to $1.7M/month in 6 months; Gym Launch, $0 to $4.4M/month in 20 months; Skool, "even better".
- The 15 plays in one line each:
- **Attraction:**
- Win Your Money Back (hit the goal, get money or credit back).
- Giveaway (grand prize plus discounted runner-up offer).
- Decoy (cheap or free version next to a premium one).
- Buy X Get Y Free.
- Pay Less Now or Pay More Later.
- Free with Consumption.
- **Upsell** (whatever you offer next):
- Classic: you can't have X without Y.
- Menu: unsell, prescribe, A/B, card on file.
- Anchor: most expensive first, then the cheaper acceptable one.
- Rollover: credit what they spent toward the next thing.
- **Downsell** (whatever you offer after a no):
- Payment plan: half now, half later.
- Trial with penalty: free if you do X, Y, Z.
- Feature downsell: no guarantee, $400 off.
- **Continuity:**
- Bonus: sign up today and get X.
- Discount: free time placed at the front, end, spread or hybrid.
- Waived fee.
- Cut plays covered elsewhere: "Pick your price", "Freemium" (software).
- **Build in stages:** get customers reliably → make them pay for themselves → make them pay for other customers → maximize LTV → print money.

lessons.t: Money Models 32 — Final Words (6 min)
lessons.md:
- Ray Dalio's loop: audacious goals → failure → learn principles → improve → bigger goals. Alex shares what has worked across several businesses past $100M in enterprise value.
- Reading from a note written on his second private-jet flight (paraphrased): to every entrepreneur disappointing the people who doubt them, he's their biggest fan. You can't lose if you don't quit. Feeling hopeless or like a disappointment means you're on the path. Keep taking one more step, one more call, one more sale. He's felt 100% confidence and 1,000% doubt at the same time. Success is the only revenge.
- Mission: real business education for everyone. Dying without sharing what you know wastes it, and your success helps him achieve his.
- Resources: acquisition.com (scale or sell buttons for $1M+ profit companies), free Offers and Leads books and trainings, an avatar chapter, careers page.
