## Business Models & Monetization

202 ideas from 111 videos. [#N] = video N in the Start here tab.

- Big macro effects he predicts: lower costs of production, pressure on capitalism and employment, experiments with universal basic income, faster science (possibly fusion), and disruption of dating and relationships via AI companions. [▶ 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KYqEK_T_5M4)
- Sell your "sawdust": combine assets you already pay for into new products with no extra operational drag, e.g. using his portfolio team to run workshops for smaller companies, or renting gym space during idle midday hours. Double-dip by turning work you must do anyway into content. [▶ 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRMG_HpOAN4)
- Four forms of leverage: labor, capital (both need permission), code and content/media (permissionless, near-zero replication cost). Each jump roughly 10x'd his income: employee, self-employed trainer, gym owner (labor), licensing (labor plus media), then adding capital via acquisitions. [▶ 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qxQIcDrre1E)
- Only six base things can be sold: products, services, access, media, risk and money, each physical or digital. Add one to your stack without operational drag; e.g. his agency licensed its winning ads monthly to DIY clients for roughly an extra $1M/month profit. [▶ 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qxQIcDrre1E)
- Income comes from the value of the problem you solve; the bigger the gap between a customer's problem and your solution, the more you can charge and keep. [▶ 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dZ7xeVCYC5M)
- A business is an arbitrage between the cost to acquire a customer and what that customer is worth. Either sell very expensive things to a few or very cheap things to everyone; the middle is where businesses die. Starting high (like Tesla's $250k Roadster before the Model 3) funds the move down-market later. [▶ 13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI)
- The only way to do purely what you love is to stay unscalable: make only as much as you want, when you want, and raise prices as demand grows. Otherwise it is fine to earn money in one field and keep your passion separate (he runs a non-profit gym with no members). [▶ 15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UDBkiBnMrHs)
- New product lines grew from adjacent needs customers revealed: a teacher using the book led to a high-school curriculum used in roughly 48% of US high schools; employers' demand led to a workplace version (SmartDollar) used by about 10,000 companies. Diverse lines plateauing at different times kept total growth smooth. [▶ 21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jvXOOddDg_s)
- Rough revenue mix he gave: about 40% from endorsed/trusted partner and advertising programs, roughly 15% EntreLeadership, 15% Financial Peace University, under 10% the EveryDollar app, with publishing and events mainly lead generators. He deliberately sells no financial products (insurance, investments) to keep advice credible. [▶ 21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jvXOOddDg_s)
- Client-financed acquisition: structure your offers so a new customer's first-30-day cash pays back their CAC, their cost of goods, and the CAC of the next customer. His rule of thumb: 30-day gross profit of at least 2x CAC. Thirty days matters because credit cards give interest-free float for that long; a shorter cash cycle lets you repeat the loop more often each month. [▶ 25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k-3PoOT4vOM)
- Vehicle choice changes the outcome: the same unit economics are worth far more in a business valued on revenue (10x top line) than in one valued on profit (around 7x EBITDA). Building enterprise value that you don't cash out grows tax-free, which is a bigger lever than chasing tax loopholes on cash income. [▶ 25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k-3PoOT4vOM)
- In a cash crisis, make one bet with the shortest path to cash, timed to the buying season. Summer camp was chosen over a season pass because parents book now and the slow season follows. Plan to pull forward enough cash to survive the off-season, then pour that cash back into ads. [▶ 26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xRxVpjeHmeA)
- Money only comes from voluntary exchange, so give value first. Ways to earn: resell or deliver other people's products at a margin for convenience, make your own, or sell skills and outcomes. Affiliate, referral and ambassador programs are an easy way to learn selling, because you only need one skill: promotion. [▶ 32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oys_fv25SYM)
- Convert payment plans into recurring revenue automatically when the plan ends. A $300/month membership sold as a $10K program with long financing raised average stay from 3 to 8 months. [▶ 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JE2_7elAcxM)
- LTV (lifetime gross profit, not revenue) to CAC is the single most important metric; aim for at least 3:1 and try to recover CAC within 30 days, using an upfront charge if needed. Estimate LTV as last year's gross profit divided by customers. Starbucks' roughly $14K LTV supports enormous ad spend. His biggest wins came from 30:1 to 200:1 windows, which you should pour money into while they last. [▶ 36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=reisEL_D7xc)
- Pivot to the work others ignore. Repairs (about $1.5K ticket, 64% gross margin) are jobs competitors won't bother with. Bundle all non-replacement work to lift the repair ticket to $2.5-5K and build a high-volume, systemized repair machine with steadier revenue, shorter sales cycles, more reps, no insurance delays and no cash-flow crunch; replacements come as upsells. Result: services went from 15-20 to 60-80 per month, with techs doing 3-5 jobs a day. [▶ 40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU)
- Client-financed acquisition: make enough on the first sale to cover the cost to acquire and fulfill that customer plus the next one. Then capital stops being a constraint, each customer funds two more, and you can outspend competitors. [▶ 48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mqqbuM9sAk)
- Prestige Labs sold supplements through the gym-owner base: 1.7M in its first full month, physical products with no extra fulfillment for gyms, gym-only distribution, 30% higher prices on the public site, and subscriptions (a second recurring charge per member). It cost about $4M to launch ($1M on custom POS and kiosk tech) and was hit by supply-chain and legal risks plus low consumer stickiness. [▶ 48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mqqbuM9sAk)
- Software lessons: keep an in-house CTO instead of outsourced dev shops; run pricing surveys early (repackaging how they charged unlocked about 4x pricing power); align incentives with every stakeholder (pay per show); and maximize appointment availability (days, hours, slots), which can swing results 50-200%. [▶ 48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mqqbuM9sAk)
- Semi-private beats one-on-one: charge about two-thirds of the one-on-one rate to groups of about 8. One-on-one at $60/hour for 4 hours is $240; 8 students at $35 each is $280/hour, about $1,120 per 4-hour day (about 4.5x more per hour). [▶ 49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CGSd00h-6zI)
- You don't need money to make money. One route: sell a large company a result worth $5-10M and take a cut, e.g. promise a $100M/year e-commerce brand a 5% conversion lift (about $5M) in exchange for 1% of revenue (about $1M). If you lack the skill, accept that and go learn it. [▶ 52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sLXhCDRaV8)
- Affiliate products you genuinely love: honestly test many options and recommend the best one, which saves your audience time and earns you commission with no inventory or upfront cost. [▶ 52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sLXhCDRaV8)
- Arbitrage: sell the same thing in two markets priced differently (e.g. crypto that is cheaper in one country's exchange, physical goods, or borrowing at 1% and lending at 6%). Wealthy people think in terms of capturing a share of the value they create, not dollars per hour. [▶ 52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sLXhCDRaV8)
- Partnerships: only partner with someone who brings money, experience or time and energy you lack, and their contribution must be clearly defined. He had nine failed partnerships before the one with Leila worked. [▶ 56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vhOV_Od0A3M)
- Your earnings are value created x your ability to negotiate your share x how replaceable you are. Uniqueness comes from your particular stack of skills, which nobody can copy without living your path. [▶ 56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vhOV_Od0A3M)
- Good business partners are rare (you can count them on one hand), and many applicant businesses are held back by the wrong partnership. Leila persistently brought evidence that operations, culture and people matter. [▶ 60](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hCgr7jT7JLA)
- Tactics (a DM trick, a hashtag hack) go stale fast; what lasts is the underlying unit economics of the business. Fix the model before hunting for new methods. [▶ 62](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7bLRKwKSms)
- Track two numbers: gross profit per customer within 30 days (the usual cash-float limit, and roughly the interest-free credit card window), and the cost to acquire a customer (ads, content, commissions; not delivery cost). [▶ 62](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7bLRKwKSms)
- Quick yearly estimates: CAC = total acquisition spend / new customers. Lifetime gross profit = (revenue / customers) minus (delivery cost / customers). Averages over a full year smooth out good and bad months. [▶ 62](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7bLRKwKSms)
- Optimize the ratio, not the lowest CAC: $5,000 LTV at $500 CAC (10:1) beats $1,000 at $200 (5:1). Paying more for higher-value customers often widens the ratio, and the payback period decides how fast you can reinvest. [▶ 62](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7bLRKwKSms)
- Raising capital fits businesses with big upfront costs, rising margins later, or winner-take-all network effects (platforms, marketplaces, pharma, manufacturing). It lets you hire top people, outspend rivals, lose money on acquisition, and face fewer well-funded competitors. Skool is his venture-backed example, priced at about $9/month. [▶ 67](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ)
- The costs of raising: you now serve two customers (end users and investors), your equity gets diluted, liquidation preferences and ratchets can shrink a founder's payout (his partner's first exit), board seats can lead to you being voted out, and VCs need swing-for-the-fences outcomes while you only get one life. Many founders spend 5-10 years and end up with nothing. [▶ 67](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ)
- Turn down opportunistic side deals, such as an agency taking equity in one client. Odd one-off arrangements drag down efficiency in the core business, and investors see them as a sign of an undisciplined founder. He counts starting the supplement company alongside gyms as one of his mistakes. [▶ 69](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ueJg14gQLuc)
- Barbell strategy: on one side go fully AI-native, including the hard team conversations. On the other, bet on things that won't change (a Bezos idea): health and fitness, food and consumables, housing, and entertainment, which should boom as leisure time grows (e.g., AI-made films). Adult content tends to adopt tech first and is a leading indicator. [▶ 73](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9q5ojtkqsBs)
- Do a few things well, like Raising Cane's: the menu is tenders, fries, Texas toast, coleslaw, sauce and drinks (the "sandwich" is tenders on toast). The founder owns every location and became a billionaire. If doing one thing well would make everything else irrelevant, stop letting everything else matter. [▶ 75](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XwzU4RikbGs)
- Sell to people who are valuable because of who they are. A CRO agency adding 10% for a $1M store creates $100k (charging $36k), but the same work for a $100M store creates $10M and could earn $3.6M. Parables: a clunker car offered $500 by the scrapyard and $100k by a collector; a stranger whose mortgage was paid off after he pushed a stalled car that turned out to belong to a billionaire. [▶ 77](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4GjwtnA76ig)
- Harvard and "make $10k/month in 30 days" courses both sell education. Four things separate a trusted education brand from one that looks like a scam: selective admission, data-based expectations, giving the knowledge away while selling implementation, and not passing everyone. [▶ 78](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oTQPxPFROck)
- The flywheel: even 25 elite graduates in year one create demand from employers and from their friends (e.g., top salespeople earning about $300k versus a ~$60k industry average), which supports premium pricing for a one-year program backed by real outcome data. [▶ 78](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oTQPxPFROck)
- Case: a luxury personal styling business at about $309k revenue, $130k profit (42% margin), 40 active clients and only 1 churned in a year. It charges $8,500 for 60-day onboarding (assessment, closet teardown, inventory, 5-10 new outfits), then $2k/month or $4.5k/quarter, plus about 10% commission on clothing. Blended CAC is about $600 against roughly $10k LTV (16:1). With strong economics, the job is simply more volume. [▶ 79](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nrounb8NlFQ)
- Four types of leverage (from Naval's Almanack): labor, capital, code and media. Code and media need a one-time effort but serve unlimited people, and compounding is leverage over time (Buffett's snowball). He realized his businesses had nothing that compounded and picked media as the lever that best fit his skills. [▶ 80](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6DCDGSnRDtM)
- Sell in a vacuum so you don't compete on price. There are two routes: sell where nobody else sells (the "where"), or sell something nobody else offers (the "what"). Strong inbound demand also creates a vacuum, because buyers choose between you and doing nothing. [▶ 82](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FMzKk73iUhw)
- His fastest restart playbook: find a local business with a high-ticket service, negotiate a bulk rate for a large batch of customers (for example, 100 chiropractic clients), pay for the marketing yourself, sell and work the leads yourself, and keep the spread while the business does the delivery. It is zero risk for them, and it made him about $100K in a month after he went broke. [▶ 83](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U_s0ekwPK5g)
- Agency and coaching lessons: productize and niche hard so non-experts can deliver from playbooks. Gym Launch served only micro gyms with at least 30 members, a lease and an employee. Price small-business services for the client's worst month, not their best. One example is a fully automated $300/month SEO and reviews service. Bigger clients churn less and make you harder to replace. [▶ 83](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U_s0ekwPK5g)
- Pool your customers' purchasing power. By negotiating payments, domains and shipping as if all merchants were one giant retailer, Shopify passed the savings on (keeping a small margin), which led to Payments, Capital and similar products. Partner with specialists for side projects (Shopify sold its logistics arm to Flexport) and stay focused on the core business. [▶ 95](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YZdE8U5eD_s)
- There are three kinds of things you can sell, each physical or digital, for six categories: products (supplements vs. a streaming subscription), services (massage vs. a marketing agency), and access (concert tickets vs. a private Slack or virtual event with the expert). [▶ 96](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m-7VjocC76M)
- Margins and scalability vary by type. Digital access and digital products have almost 100% margins. Services are hard to scale because people, culture, training and onboarding all have to grow with them, which is why buyers value service businesses less. Adding more categories raises enterprise value. [▶ 96](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m-7VjocC76M)
- Venture capital can push a workable, profitable small business into a "billion or bust" model it was never suited for; ButcherBox's founder's prior marketplace raised repeatedly, burned about $500K/month, and he ended up owning around 8% before it was foreclosed. VCs earn management fees on deployed capital, so their incentive is to get you to spend more, not to be profitable. [▶ 101](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=orMbq2LtzKE)
- Run on one unit metric everyone knows: dollars of fully loaded gross profit per box (meat, packing, box, shipping, dry ice, card fees, even tape). Target was ~$20/box at launch so affiliate payouts stayed first-box profitable; current targets are ~30% gross margin and ~6% net. Typical split: ~10% of revenue to operations, ~20% left for marketing or profit. [▶ 101](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=orMbq2LtzKE)
- Results on that service line: recurring share went from 9% to 60%, memberships from roughly 0% to 30%, visits per customer from about 2 to 4-6, and monthly recurring revenue from about $20K to over $250K, more than 10x, just from repackaging and a new sales process. [▶ 105](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UhvBSQFy6A)
- The key number is the ratio of lifetime gross profit (what people loosely call LTV) to customer acquisition cost (CAC). It shows how much you get back for each dollar spent acquiring customers and predicts how far you can scale ads, how profitable you'll be and how many customers you can buy. A 100:1 ratio means you can be 10x less efficient and still earn 10:1. [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- LTV must be gross profit, not revenue: subtract delivery costs. Example: an ads agency charging $2,000/month with a 5-month average stay (20% churn, so $2,000 / 0.20 = $10,000) thought it had 5:1 returns, but $1,000/month went to client ad spend and each $5,000/month rep handled only 5 accounts ($1,000/account), leaving zero gross profit. [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- Service businesses often forget delivery payroll is cost of goods: divide delivery payroll by customers served (e.g. one hire per five clients) to get delivery cost per customer and model it at scale. Fixed overhead like rent stays out of gross profit. [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- CAC = all sales and marketing payroll + ad spend + commissions over a period, divided by new customers (e.g. $10K ads + $10K payroll / 20 customers = $1,000). Using a full year smooths out volatility. [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- Young businesses can estimate LTV from one month of churn: if 9 of 10 customers remain after 30 days, churn is 10%, so LTV is about price / 0.10, i.e. a 10-month average stay. [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- When the ratio is huge, rising CAC barely matters: Starbucks' lifetime value per customer is around $14,000 while a local food-business customer may cost ~$10 (his cookie-shop ads cost under $1 per lead with 1 in 10 showing up), so CAC could rise severalfold and still print money. A strong ratio lets you reach colder audiences and new channels and outbid competitors in ad auctions, an ethical moat. [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- Levers to raise LTV: raise price, cut delivery cost, increase purchase frequency, cross-sell, upsell to a better version, sell more units, and down-sell a cheaper or smaller version to turn a no into a yes. Pick whichever creates the least operational drag (asking buyers to buy another copy beats writing a second book). [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- CAC for a given customer type is roughly similar across competitors; long-term winners are the ones who stack more LTV. If an activity doesn't get customers cheaper or make them worth more, it's probably wasted time. [▶ 106](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzKpAtzKQ54)
- Economics: BDRs paid ~$50 per shown appointment and about 10% of shown SDS calls close, so roughly $500 in BDR cost per sale against a ~$40K LTV. [▶ 107](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=okA9Yt2KZuk)
- Supply and demand is the strongest force in business. Know which side constrains you: supply-constrained businesses (cleaning, accounting, legal, niche consulting, trades) are really in the recruiting business, while demand-constrained ones (e-commerce, B2B software, weight loss, music lessons) must win at getting customers. [▶ 108](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cnbHgYYHzyE)
- Look for "sawdust": waste or spare capacity that can become a new product (plywood from mill sawdust; unused office space turned into on-site workshops that generate deal flow, cash, content and talent). Look for assets that check several boxes at once, like turning internal SOPs into lead magnets. [▶ 108](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cnbHgYYHzyE)
- Results within ~90 days: profit 5% to 30%, revenue retention 2% to 30%, ascensions from 0-1 to 5-6 per month, ~$2M of added EBITDA. Most profit is made on the back end; build back to front so you can later outspend competitors on acquisition. Don't scale ads until the "bucket" stops leaking, and stay close enough to know where the problems in each department are. [▶ 109](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QTZsh3BgOwY)
- Every business takes on debt: venture-backed firms take financial debt to hire talent at market rates; bootstrappers take "management debt" and do the work of several people through the "swamp" until they can afford help. Don't copy the habits rich people adopted after getting rich (like flying private); they aren't how they got there. [▶ 110](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H_ZLs1-jOKQ)
- Self-publishing and selling through his own store instead of Amazon: Amazon caps a new book's initial hardcover stock (~5-10K), he wanted full ownership of the content (traditional publishers take the rights), and he wanted freedom to give chapters away or price the earlier book at $1.99, which publishers wouldn't allow. He fronted printing, warehousing and shipping himself. [▶ 111](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qel9bf653Es)
- Results: about 100,000 books sold the first day (the previous book sold just under 500K in two years), top chart positions for the audiobook and podcast, and his name trending. He thinks more people believe they have a leads problem than an offer problem, so the leads book could outsell the offers book. [▶ 111](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qel9bf653Es)
